bwyKH7kyvrU.title: Stages of the Hereafter 5: Death, Part 3
bwyKH7kyvrU.one_line: Death is a calamity and each person's own Day of Judgement; rehearse your last day, love meeting Allah, and do not be fooled by the dunya.
bwyKH7kyvrU.summary: He teaches that a believer should not wish for death, but if he must, he asks Allah to keep him alive while life is good for him and take him when death is better. The Quran calls death a calamity: the doer of good loses the chance to do more, and the sinner loses the chance to repent. Each person's death is his own personal Day of Judgement, more pressing than abstract talk about the signs of the Hour. He wants listeners to grow comfortable with death so they prepare for it, and suggests imagining today is your last day, as an early pious man did by lying in the dark beside his bed and speaking to himself as if dead. Everything perishes except Allah; no human was granted immortality, not even the Prophet; death was created before life, and no extra moment is granted when the term comes. He explains the hadith about loving to meet Allah, Umm Habibah's dua for long life, and Jibreel's counsel to live as you wish because you will die. He closes with a caliph's sermon after a funeral, the point that death will always feel too early, and a companion's saying about three things that make him laugh and three that make him cry.

outline.heading: Opening
Do not wish for death: the prophetic dua
outline.gist: Instead of wishing for death, ask Allah to keep you alive as long as life is good for you and to take you when death is better.

outline.heading: The Quran calls death a calamity
outline.gist: Even from a religious view death is the ultimate misfortune; the Quran names it the calamity of death.

outline.heading: Why death is a calamity
outline.gist: If you were doing well, you lose the chance to grow closer to Allah; if not, you lose the chance to turn back that was open to you every moment.

outline.heading: Your death is your personal Day of Judgement
outline.gist: There is a general Hour for everyone, but each person's own resurrection begins the day they die, which matters more than abstract talk about signs of the Hour.

outline.heading: Grow comfortable with death to prepare for it
outline.gist: Familiarity with death makes proper preparation more likely, and preparation makes the transition easier.

outline.heading: An early pious man rehearsing his own death
outline.gist: He would lie in the dark between his bed and the wall, tell himself he had died and the time for deeds was over, then rise thanking Allah for another chance.

outline.heading: Imagine today is your last day
outline.gist: Ask what you would do, say to loved ones, which ties you would mend, and how you would pray and fast; you have no real reason to believe tomorrow is coming.

outline.heading: Everything perishes except Allah; even the Prophet died
outline.gist: No human before the Prophet was granted immortality, and if the beloved Prophet died, no one is entitled to more.

outline.heading: Death was created before life
outline.gist: Allah created death and life, death first: lifelessness is the natural state of everything, and any life is granted by His will.

outline.heading: Only Allah lives without dying
outline.gist: The Prophet's dua addresses Allah as the Ever-Living who sustains Himself while all creation dies.

outline.heading: No extra moment, and the angel entrusted with you
outline.gist: The verses the imam recited in prayer: the dying ask for a short delay to give charity and are refused; the angel of death takes each soul at a moment decreed long before.

outline.heading: Loving to meet Allah
outline.gist: Whoever loves to meet Allah, Allah loves to meet him. Aisha worried because everyone dislikes death; the Prophet explained that at death the believer is given glad tidings and longs to meet Allah, while the disbeliever is shown what awaits him.

outline.heading: Umm Habibah's dua for long life
outline.gist: She asked to enjoy the company of her husband the Prophet, her father and her brother; he told her that asking refuge from the punishment of the grave and the Fire would have been better, since lifespans are already set.

outline.heading: Jibreel's counsel: live as you wish, you will die
outline.gist: Jibreel told the Prophet that whatever one does, death comes; the believer's honour lies in standing at night and his dignity in not needing people.

outline.heading: A caliph's sermon after a funeral
outline.gist: After a janazah a well-known caliph spoke about the grave in a long, moving address he quotes in parts.

outline.heading: It will always feel too early
outline.gist: At twenty or seventy death will feel premature; accepting it is psychological, like going without coffee calmly in Ramadan, and acceptance helps you deal with it.

outline.heading: Status, wealth and youth all end
outline.gist: The caliph's warning: the powerful are humbled, the wealthy lose their wealth, the young grow old, so do not be fooled by how quickly the dunya gives.

outline.heading: Which of my cheeks will decay first?
outline.gist: Imagining himself in the grave, the caliph asked which cheek would decay first and what the angel of death would bring him from Allah, then wept; he died that week.

outline.heading: What makes him laugh: the planner with death at the door
outline.gist: A companion laughed at one who plans for years while death waits at his door.

outline.heading: What makes him laugh: the heedless who is not ignored
outline.gist: One oblivious to reality while reality is not oblivious to him.

outline.heading: What makes him laugh: laughter without knowing Allah's pleasure
outline.gist: One who laughs loudly with no idea whether he is pleasing Allah.

outline.heading: What makes him cry: losing the Prophet and his companions
outline.gist: Remembering the loss of the Prophet and those who lived like him.

outline.heading: What makes him cry: the terror at death
outline.gist: The frightening, uncertain moment when death arrives.

outline.heading: What makes him cry: standing before Allah
outline.gist: Standing before Allah with everything exposed, not knowing which way he will go.

outline.heading: Outro

8r-80z3JRM8.title: The Empty Space Ep. 7: Sins and Solutions Part 2, with Q&A
8r-80z3JRM8.one_line: Envy and its cure through seeing others as teammates, brief notes on selfishness and lust, then a long Q&A on purifying the nafs.
8r-80z3JRM8.summary: He completes the four major diseases with envy, distinguishing it from healthy wishing for good. He rejects the superstition that surrounds envy and the evil eye: protect yourself with Quran, adhkar and dua, still see a doctor, and stop parading blessings, especially on social media. Envy does real harm when the envious person acts on it, as in a friend who quietly wrecks an engagement. Its roots lie in the nafs's urge to be on top, so he offers three correctives: another's success is not your failure since every life follows its own storyline, Allah's blessings are limitless, and Allah asks only for your best, not to beat others. The cure is the Islamic concept of jama'ah: we wear the same jersey, so others' success is the ummah's win. He touches on selfishness, which should be redirected toward Jannah, and lust as a strong instinct to be controlled. The Q&A covers recommended books, taking benefit from imperfect speakers, competition, arrogance toward non-Muslims, CBT, teaching children about the nafs, laziness as lack of ambition, healthy versus pathological guilt, entitlement, khushu as reaching the stage of love, gentleness over self-punishment, and why support groups and mentors are needed.

outline.heading: Opening
Envy versus wishing for good
outline.gist: Wishing to have what others have, if beneficial, is fine; envy is wanting others to lose their blessings or resenting their success.

outline.heading: Superstition around envy and the evil eye
outline.gist: Envy is real but unmeasurable, so blaming illness or failure on someone's eye is baseless and wasteful.

outline.heading: Protection the Prophetic way
outline.gist: Recite Quran, keep adhkar and dua, and still take the sick person to a doctor.

outline.heading: Do not parade your blessings
outline.gist: Share successes only with those who love you; social media display, often false, provokes envy.

outline.heading: How envy really harms: the broken engagement
outline.gist: An envious friend speaks badly of the groom to the bride's father; envy harms through actions, not energy from the eyes.

outline.heading: The root of envy in the nafs
outline.gist: The instinct to be strongest makes others' success feel like a threat.

outline.heading: First corrective: others' success is not your failure
outline.gist: Everyone lives a different storyline and arrives at different times; resentment while idle is really lack of ambition.

outline.heading: Second corrective: Allah's blessings are limitless
outline.gist: The nafs fears there is not enough to go round; reinforce the opposite through dhikr, dua and contemplation.

outline.heading: Third corrective: you are asked for your best, not to be first
outline.gist: Allah wants you to reach your own potential with the hand you were dealt.

outline.heading: Envy grows out of arrogance
outline.gist: When someone outdoes the person who believes he is better, he becomes envious and hunts for their flaws.

outline.heading: The cure: we wear the same jersey
outline.gist: Jama'ah teaches that the ummah, and humanity, is one team, so good players around you are a gain.

outline.heading: Competing while wanting everyone to finish
outline.gist: Healthy competition pushes effort while hoping all reach the goal; the ummah's success is the priority.

outline.heading: Selfishness redirected toward Jannah
outline.gist: Selfishness cannot be removed but can be aimed at Paradise, which requires selflessness in this world.

outline.heading: Lust as a powerful instinct
outline.gist: Lust, intense especially for men, cannot be removed but can be controlled and limited to avoid haram.

outline.heading: Interlude
Q: recommended books on purifying the heart
outline.gist: Al-Ghazali's Ihya with a teacher, simpler classical texts, the Hikam, a modern work on dhikr and dua, and English books on purification of the heart.

outline.heading: Q: learning from speakers with flawed views
outline.gist: Take what benefits and leave the rest; the take-all-or-leave-all attitude to scholars has done great harm.

outline.heading: Q: is competition allowed?
outline.gist: Competing in a specific domain is fine; arrogance is believing you are better as a person overall.

outline.heading: Q: arrogance toward non-Muslims
outline.gist: Using Islam to look down on people is the worst misuse of the deen; no one knows how anyone's life will end.

outline.heading: Q: convincing the nafs of the long term
outline.gist: Repeated dhikr, dua, contemplation and lessons sink in over years.

outline.heading: Q: dua in any language
outline.gist: Dua can be made in any language.

outline.heading: Q: cognitive behavioural therapy
outline.gist: CBT applies the same thought-feeling-behaviour cycle and is a powerful tool worth engaging in.

outline.heading: Q: introducing the nafs to young people
outline.gist: Explain where urges come from, especially after mistakes, so they learn to observe and resist them.

outline.heading: Q: attention-seeking versus showing off
outline.gist: Needing attention to function can reflect deeper psychological deficits needing professional help; riya is milder.

outline.heading: Q: hypocrisy as the sum of the diseases
outline.gist: Nifaq is the outcome of all these diseases together, the disease in the heart.

outline.heading: Q: finding a mentor
outline.gist: Seek someone older and more experienced; working as a group also helps.

outline.heading: Q: laziness and the cure of ambition
outline.gist: Laziness comes from the nafs refusing effort without quick reward; ambition built through ambitious company and stories of the great cures it.

outline.heading: Q: teaching pre-adolescent children
outline.gist: Ask children why they acted, name the nafs gently and patiently; grandparents often grasp this best.

outline.heading: Q: guilt and shame
outline.gist: Some guilt is the healthy voice of conscience, but motivating only by shame and guilt is harmful.

outline.heading: When guilt becomes pathological
outline.gist: Extreme guilt can stem from mental health issues and needs professional care, not more spiritual pressure.

outline.heading: Q: entitlement
outline.gist: Entitlement mixes vanity and arrogance with a lack of gratitude; experience among people with nothing often cures it.

outline.heading: Q: books of stories of the righteous
outline.gist: Classical collections exist but some contain harmful stories, so curated editions are better.

outline.heading: Q: increasing khushu in prayer
outline.gist: Khushu comes naturally at the stage of love; we move between stages and aim to stay longest in the highest.

outline.heading: Q: harshness or self-compassion when falling short
outline.gist: Harsh punishment rarely works; find the cause, make up what was missed, and stay gentle and gradual.

outline.heading: Q: are there more than four stages?
outline.gist: Higher stages exist for the elite; scholars describe up to fifteen or sixteen, all consistent in substance.

outline.heading: Q: why pleasure is an instinct
outline.gist: Science is still unsure why we play; pleasure lowers stress and ties to survival, and animals also overeat without limits.

outline.heading: Interlude
Change needs practice and support groups
outline.gist: Theory must be paired with practice, mentorship and group support to complete the journey.

outline.heading: Outro

SdrhbzjY3so.title: Stages of the Hereafter: Death of the Disbeliever (Day 11)
SdrhbzjY3so.one_line: The second half of the long narration on death: how the disbeliever's soul is taken, questioned and confined, and the loneliness of the grave.
SdrhbzjY3so.summary: Continuing the long authentic narration of what happens at death, he turns from the believer to the disbeliever and the one who went astray. Dark, stern angels descend with sackcloth from Jahannam, the angel of death calls the wicked soul out to its Lord's displeasure, and the soul, knowing what awaits, spreads through the body and is torn out. It rises with a foul stench under the worst name the person was ever called, the gates of the sky stay shut, its record is placed in the lowest register and it is returned to the earth. In the grave the person stumbles over every question, the grave closes in on him, his evil deeds appear as a repulsive companion, and he is shown the place in Jannah he lost before it is sealed. He then reflects on the loneliness of the grave: mourners walk away, visits and memories fade within a few years, and all that remains is who you were and what you did, with prayer, fasting and charity as the only company. He recounts the Prophet's dream of punishments in the barzakh, explains why the Prophet's face changed whenever he spoke of the grave, and closes by introducing the angel holding the horn.

outline.heading: Opening
The long narration on death, part two
outline.gist: One of the few very long authentic narrations; having covered the believer, he now turns to the disbeliever and the one who went astray.

outline.heading: Angels of punishment descend
outline.gist: Dark, stern angels bring sackcloth from Jahannam and sit as far as the dying person can see. Sometimes the dying cry out at what only they can see, and the angel of death sits at the head.

outline.heading: The wicked soul torn out
outline.gist: Called out to the displeasure of its Lord, the soul spreads through the body and is yanked out like a skewer pulled through wet wool. It resists because it knows what comes next, and the angels wrap it at once in sackcloth instead of a shroud of Jannah.

outline.heading: Refused at the first sky
outline.gist: It rises with a foul stench under the worst name the person was ever called, and the gates of the sky stay shut, as the Prophet recited from Al-A'raf.

outline.heading: Recorded in the lowest register and returned to earth
outline.gist: Allah commands his record be placed in the lowest register and that he be returned to the earth he was created from and will be raised from.

outline.heading: The questioning in the grave
outline.gist: Asked about his Lord, his faith and the man sent to him, he stumbles and can only say he does not know or half-remembers the name people used. A call declares him a liar and a door to Jahannam is opened for him.

outline.heading: The grave closes in and his deeds appear
outline.gist: The grave tightens until his bones press into each other, and a foul, ugly figure brings him bad news and reveals itself as his own evil deeds.

outline.heading: Shown the place he lost in Jannah
outline.gist: A door to Jannah is opened to show where he would have been had he obeyed Allah, then closed forever.

outline.heading: The grave as the first stage
outline.gist: He spends his time begging that the Hour not come, because what follows is worse. If the grave is eased, every later stage is easier; if it is hard, everything after is harder.

outline.heading: Left alone and forgotten
outline.gist: The deceased hears the footsteps of the mourners leaving. However long people stay or visit, they move on, and within a few years his name is mentioned once a year at most.

outline.heading: Only who you were remains
outline.gist: If life feels lonely, the grave is lonelier, because all that is left is who you were and what you did. For the believer, prayer sits at the head, fasting on one side and charity on the other.

outline.heading: The Prophet's dream of punishments in the barzakh
outline.gist: Two angels take the Prophet to the Holy Land and show him a man whose head is crushed by a rock, a man swimming in a river of blood and people burning from below, telling him to keep walking.

outline.heading: The punishments explained, and the Prophet's fear
outline.gist: The angels name each sin, such as lying and holding the Quran without living by it. This is why the Prophet's face changed when he spoke of the grave, and we should react the same way.

outline.heading: The angel holding the horn
outline.gist: After the grave comes the next stage: an angel holds the horn waiting for the command, and the Prophet asked how he could enjoy life knowing this. The first blow will end all existence.

quran.point: The gates of the sky are not opened for the disbeliever's soul, and they will not enter Jannah until a thick rope passes through the eye of a needle.
From the earth We created you, to it We return you and from it We raise you again: the reason the soul is sent back to earth.

hadith.gist: The long narration of al-Bara' ibn Azib on what happens at death, here the part on the disbeliever: dark angels with sackcloth, the soul torn out, refused at the sky, failing the questions, the grave narrowing and his deeds appearing as an ugly man.
The grave is the first stage of the hereafter; whoever is saved from it finds what follows easier, and whoever is not finds what follows harder.
The deceased hears the footsteps of the people walking away from the grave.
In the grave the believer's prayer comes to his head, his fasting to one side and his charity to the other to protect him.
The Prophet's dream in which two angels showed him punishments in the barzakh, including the head crushed with a rock, the river of blood and the burning oven, then explained the sin behind each.
How can I enjoy life when the angel of the horn has put it to his mouth and is waiting to be commanded to blow?

maxims: Think life is lonely? Try the grave.
All you're left with is who you were and what you did.

stories.who: The Prophet's dream of the barzakh
stories.point: The punishments he was shown were tied to sins people commit daily, and the memory shaped how he spoke of the grave for the rest of his life.

takeaways: Prepare for the grave now, since ease there makes every later stage easier.
Build the deeds that will keep you company in the grave: prayer, the fasting you are doing now, and charity.
Live for who you are before Allah rather than for being remembered, since people forget the dead within a few years.
Let the mention of the grave affect you the way it affected the Prophet, and avoid lying and neglecting the Quran.

eCLnMiecbhs.title: Stages of the Hereafter 1: Good and Bad Endings
eCLnMiecbhs.one_line: Opening a series on the hereafter, he stresses death's certainty and the weight of a good ending, with seerah and classical examples.
eCLnMiecbhs.summary: He launches a series on the stages of the hereafter because death is the one undisputed certainty, yet he regularly sees people meet it completely unprepared. The companions were at ease with death because they listened to the Prophet and read a Quran whose constant backdrop is the hereafter; avoiding the subject is denial, and denial is never healthy. His first topic is the good ending, both frightening and comforting. A superb prayer is voided if wudu breaks just before the salam, and the last metres of a race decide much of it. He then gives examples of bad endings: an early emigrant to Abyssinia who abandoned Islam, a celebrated fighter whom the Prophet said was bound for the Fire and who took his own life, a young companion unable to say the shahadah until his mother forgave him, and a shopkeeper who died repeating a line about the woman he tried to abuse. Deeds are judged by the intention that starts them and the way they end, even if the middle is messy, so one should plant the sapling even as the Hour arrives. To protect one's ending he recommends secret deeds, like the imam whose scarred back revealed years of carrying food to the poor.

outline.heading: Opening
Death: the one undisputed certainty
outline.gist: He sees people meet death unprepared despite knowing of it all their lives; success, marriage and children are hopes, while death is certain and nothing can prevent it.

outline.heading: The hereafter is the backdrop of the Quran
outline.gist: The companions were at ease with death because they listened to the Prophet and read a Quran in which nearly every surah returns to the hereafter; people avoid the topic because it is uncomfortable.

outline.heading: Denying reality is never healthy
outline.gist: Facing a certain fact maturely leads to a better and more productive life; the series opens with what comes before death, the good ending.

outline.heading: The good ending: a prayer spoiled at the last moment
outline.gist: A good ending is both frightening and comforting. Imagine your best prayer ever, voided by breaking wudu just before the salam.

outline.heading: The last metres of the race
outline.gist: Life is like a long race whose final metres carry great value and colour everything before them.

outline.heading: The emigrant to Abyssinia who lost his faith
outline.gist: An early Muslim who emigrated to Abyssinia, husband of a woman who later became a Mother of the Believers, left Islam there while others held firm, and reportedly died a drunkard.

outline.heading: The celebrated fighter who took his own life
outline.gist: The companions praised a man who fought superbly and assumed he was in Paradise; the Prophet said otherwise, and he was found to have fallen on his own sword.

outline.heading: The young companion and his mother's displeasure
outline.gist: A dying young companion could not say the shahadah because his mother was unhappy with him; the Prophet ordered a fire prepared, and she forgave him to spare him.

outline.heading: The shopkeeper and the road to the bathhouse
outline.gist: A man who lured a woman asking directions and failed to assault her felt no remorse, only regret that he had not locked her in, and at death could only repeat the words about the bathhouse.

outline.heading: A dying scholar prompted to say the shahadah
outline.gist: Shy students sat around their dying teacher repeating the shahadah, hoping he would say it, until he asked whether that was why they were saying it.

outline.heading: Interlude
Deeds are judged by intention and ending
outline.gist: Two hadith look at the start and the end of deeds; the middle of life may be a mess of ups and downs, but what counts is a clear intention at the outset and refusing to give up at the last moment.

outline.heading: Plant the sapling as the Hour arrives
outline.gist: Even with the Day of Judgement upon you, plant the young tree in your hand, because it is about the note you finish on; the Prophet prayed for this and the companions kept their eyes on it.

outline.heading: Secret deeds known only to Allah
outline.gist: One of his teachers advised keeping deeds no one else knows of, not even family, and taking them to the grave.

outline.heading: The imam with the scarred back
outline.gist: When a great imam was washed after death his back was found scarred; the poor then asked who had stopped leaving food at their doors, revealing a lifetime of carrying sacks to them before Fajr.

KXCGgsdKKO8.title: The Empty Space Ep. 5: The Tools
KXCGgsdKKO8.one_line: Seven tools Islam gives for purifying the nafs: dhikr, dua, a daily Quran portion, service, night prayer, fasting and reading.
KXCGgsdKKO8.summary: Continuing his series, he explains seven tools for changing the nafs, each to be built up gently, gradually and consistently. Dhikr is the anchor: start with a small daily count, push the number up when the nafs resists until it accepts the base amount, then hold it for weeks before adding more. Dhikr also has a mind form, reflecting on the meaning of the words, and a knowledge form, listening every day to someone who reminds you of Allah, plus the Prophet's invocations for daily moments. Dua is a free daily therapy session: the nafs overhears your fears and hopes and slowly adopts them, just as people learn best from indirect advice, and your duas reveal who you are. A small daily portion of Quran should be kept like an obligation and mined for one lesson to practise. Service outside your comfort zone shrinks the ego, illustrated by an elderly scholar who poured water and arranged shoes, and by his teacher making him serve a bully who later became a close friend. Night prayer, kept private so the nafs gains no reputation from it, fasting beyond Ramadan, and reading life in the widest sense complete the kit. Ramadan, he says, is a thirty-day boot camp in all of them.

outline.heading: Opening
Why fight the nafs: diseases of the heart block a full life
outline.gist: Talking about the nafs is real, not superstition; purifying it lets you enjoy life more.

outline.heading: Tool one: dhikr, the anchor tool
outline.gist: Allah asks for abundant remembrance and the Prophet told a simple man to keep his tongue moist with it; therapy has nothing equal to it.

outline.heading: Dhikr as training the nafs
outline.gist: Scholars treat dhikr as practice for the soul and describe three types.

outline.heading: Dhikr of the tongue: start with a small daily count
outline.gist: Begin with about three hundred daily phrases of tasbih, tahmid and istighfar and hold to it.

outline.heading: Bargaining with the nafs to build the habit
outline.gist: When it resists, raise the target until it settles for the base amount, keep it for weeks, then add more.

outline.heading: Scholars who loved tens of thousands of dhikr
outline.gist: Built slowly and privately, dhikr becomes a joy; do not parade it.

outline.heading: Dhikr of the mind: reflecting on meanings
outline.gist: Think about sins when seeking forgiveness and blessings when praising; this moves the feeling-thought-behaviour cycle from within.

outline.heading: Dhikr through knowledge: daily listening
outline.gist: Listen ten to fifteen minutes daily to someone who reminds you of Allah, start small and grow it, as the Prophet spaced his lessons.

outline.heading: Building up children's Quran reading
outline.gist: Small amounts grown slowly let children read large portions with ease.

outline.heading: Invocations for daily moments and a personal litany
outline.gist: Learn the Prophet's adhkar for waking, dressing and eating, and build a daily wird such as a classical scholar's collection.

outline.heading: Tool two: dua as a daily therapy session
outline.gist: Dua is a conversation with Allah about fears and hopes, and the nafs listening to it changes its convictions.

outline.heading: People learn best from indirect advice
outline.gist: Speaking to a teddy bear or about a third person works better than direct criticism, as the Prophet did with 'what is wrong with some people'.

outline.heading: Dua is the mirror of the spirit
outline.gist: What you ask for reveals who you are; the Prophet's supplications show his character, and Quranic figures like Maryam's mother simply confide.

outline.heading: What you hear becomes your narrative
outline.gist: Repeated hopes become the nafs's own, just as music and media shape lifestyles; guard what enters your ears and eyes.

outline.heading: Five minutes of dua alone, in any language
outline.gist: Sit alone daily, even awkwardly silent at first, speak in your own language and build up; it eases anxiety.

outline.heading: Tool three: a daily portion of Quran
outline.gist: Keep even one verse daily, memorise and understand it, and make it up if missed, as the Prophet taught.

outline.heading: Find one lesson to practise from each reading
outline.gist: Each day's verses should yield one new behaviour.

outline.heading: Tool four: service outside your comfort zone
outline.gist: Serving where the nafs finds no self-interest is more sincere; he took up public speaking and medicine this way.

outline.heading: The elderly scholar who poured water
outline.gist: A scholar in his nineties served water and arranged shoes at study circles, teaching humility through service.

outline.heading: Serving the person he disliked
outline.gist: His teacher made him serve and pray for a bully for a week; his ego shrank and the man became a close friend.

outline.heading: Tool five: night prayer
outline.gist: The Prophet praised Abdullah ibn Umar on condition he prayed at night, and he never left it after.

outline.heading: Ramadan as a thirty-day boot camp
outline.gist: Ramadan trains every tool at once so that continuing them changes the nafs.

outline.heading: Keep two rakahs every night
outline.gist: After Ramadan hold to two short rakahs nightly, lengthening them rather than adding more.

outline.heading: Each movement of prayer treats a disease of the heart
outline.gist: The invocations of standing, bowing, prostrating and sitting each address an inner ailment.

outline.heading: Keep night prayer secret
outline.gist: If others know, the nafs gains reputation from it and stops being trained.

outline.heading: Tool six: fasting
outline.gist: Fasting changes body and mind and loosens food's hold; avoid huge iftars and keep Monday, Thursday or white-day fasts.

outline.heading: Tool seven: reading life
outline.gist: Learn from every person, book and experience; an educated nafs is less dangerous and its convictions change through information.

outline.heading: Outro
You cannot do this alone
outline.gist: Purification needs support, a guide and a group.

mcyGSImWUlE.speaker_note: own series The Empty Space at MWN; speaks of 'our line of work' and the earlier episodes he gave
mcyGSImWUlE.title: The Empty Space Ep. 3: The Stages
mcyGSImWUlE.one_line: How the nafs works: its two instincts, three blind spots, its convictions, and four stages of changing it toward love of obedience.
mcyGSImWUlE.summary: In the third episode of his series on the inner life, he explains the nafs as the real target of tazkiyah. The soul has two built-in goals, survival and pleasure, and every urge can be traced to them, from grabbing food at the table to gazing at what is forbidden. It is blind in three ways: it has no sense of halal and haram, it cannot see long-term harm or limits, which is why people fall into addiction, and for it the end always justifies the means. Islam does not ask us to stop being self-interested. It asks us to be supremely selfish about Jannah, and the road there is selfless service, a path of ease that only feels hard because the nafs is short-sighted. The threat of punishment is what makes the choice clear to it. Instincts cannot be changed, but convictions can: envy and arrogance grow from wrong convictions, while self-worth should be kept and rooted in being a servant Allah has trusted. He closes with four stages of change: full submission to the nafs, forcing it, its weary acceptance, and finally love, when it finds joy in prayer and disgust in sin. He urges persistent self-persuasion through reflection rather than endless force.

outline.heading: Opening
The nafs as the target of purification
outline.gist: To change and elevate the nafs we first have to understand it properly.

outline.heading: The soul's two instincts: survival and pleasure
outline.gist: Every human drive, for wealth, status, strength, children or rest, serves the nafs's two goals of keeping you alive and giving you joy.

outline.heading: Examples: grabbing food and the wandering gaze
outline.gist: The childhood urge to take the most food and men's urge to look at what is haram are the nafs trying to strengthen and preserve you.

outline.heading: First blind spot: no sense of right and wrong
outline.gist: Halal and haram mean nothing to the nafs; it urges only by its two goals.

outline.heading: Second blind spot: no long-term view or limits
outline.gist: It lives in the moment, so it overeats and is drawn into addiction, unable to weigh later harm.

outline.heading: Why Muslims must study the inner self
outline.gist: Understanding mind, spirit and soul is part of the faith and of caring for mental wellbeing, including knowing when to seek specialists.

outline.heading: Distraction as the nafs's defence
outline.gist: The nafs keeps the mind busy with games and entertainment so it is never examined critically.

outline.heading: Third blind spot: the end justifies the means
outline.gist: It does not care how it gets what it wants; turned into a philosophy this has caused endless suffering.

outline.heading: Self-interest: be selfish about Jannah
outline.gist: The nafs only acts in its own interest, and Allah wants us to be utterly selfish when it comes to Paradise.

outline.heading: Father and son drawing lots to go to battle
outline.gist: A companion tells his son he would give him anything in this world, but not his place in Jannah.

outline.heading: The road to ultimate selfishness is selfless service
outline.gist: Allah made the path to the greatest joy and survival a path of serving others; the nafs only needs to look further ahead.

outline.heading: Why punishment belongs in the equation
outline.gist: Without punishment the nafs would take pleasure now; pleasure later versus pain later makes the choice obvious to it.

outline.heading: The deen is a path of ease; the problem is the soul
outline.gist: Obligations and prohibitions are not hard in themselves; they feel hard because the nafs is short-sighted and must be purified.

outline.heading: Adam sent to earth to learn self-control
outline.gist: Creation and its trials are about learning to master the nafs; give to others to fill your account in the next life.

outline.heading: From instinct to conviction: envy and arrogance
outline.gist: The instinct to be ahead becomes a conviction that others' success is bad, which produces envy and arrogance.

outline.heading: The nafs is an ally, not an enemy
outline.gist: Its instincts kept humanity alive, like an infant crying for food; the aim is to redirect it, not destroy it.

outline.heading: Self-worth is a conviction worth keeping
outline.gist: Without self-esteem people struggle deeply; what must change is the reason behind it.

outline.heading: The nafs commands evil: where true value comes from
outline.gist: It commands evil through its means, not its goals; real worth comes from being a servant whom Allah trusted with choice and accountability.

outline.heading: How convictions are damaged and changed
outline.gist: Abuse, neglect and severe hardship can convince the nafs it is worthless; change takes long, persistent work or extreme circumstances.

outline.heading: Persuading the nafs through reflection
outline.gist: Contemplation sends positive thoughts into the heart, strengthening the spirit and conscience and slowly swaying the nafs.

outline.heading: Stage one: full submission to the nafs
outline.gist: Children and animals live by instinct; adults who stay here take their desires as their god, and knowledge alone will not fix it.

outline.heading: Stage two: forcing the nafs
outline.gist: A nourished spirit and loud conscience make us do what the nafs resists, from studying to prayer; seeing legacy as survival makes it easier.

outline.heading: Why coercion does not last
outline.gist: What is done under force tires out and becomes empty motions, as with forcing children beyond a young age.

outline.heading: Stage three: acceptance and habit
outline.gist: The nafs stops fighting but still sees no benefit, so acts become hollow routine if one stays here.

outline.heading: Stage four: love and joy in obedience
outline.gist: When its convictions change, the nafs wants good deeds as its own joy, as the Prophet found his delight in prayer.

outline.heading: Examples: quitting smoking and avoiding zina
outline.gist: Real change means looking back on sin with disgust and finding joy in halal, as the early generations did.

outline.heading: Outro

43:46.ar: وَلَقَدۡ أَرۡسَلۡنَا مُوسَىٰ بِـَٔايَٰتِنَآ إِلَىٰ فِرۡعَوۡنَ وَمَلَإِيْهِۦ فَقَالَ إِنِّي رَسُولُ رَبِّ ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ
43:46.en: And verily We sent Moses with Our revelations unto Pharaoh and his chiefs, and he said: I am a messenger of the Lord of the Worlds

43:47.ar: فَلَمَّا جَآءَهُم بِـَٔايَٰتِنَآ إِذَا هُم مِّنۡهَا يَضۡحَكُونَ
43:47.en: But when he brought them Our tokens, behold! they laughed at them

43:48.ar: وَمَا نُرِيهِم مِّنۡ ءَايَةٍ إِلَّا هِيَ أَكۡبَرُ مِنۡ أُخۡتِهَاۖ وَأَخَذۡنَٰهُم بِٱلۡعَذَابِ لَعَلَّهُمۡ يَرۡجِعُونَ
43:48.en: And every token that We showed them was greater than its sister (token), and We grasped them with the torment, that haply they might turn again

43:49.ar: وَقَالُواْ يَٰٓأَيُّهَ ٱلسَّاحِرُ ٱدۡعُ لَنَا رَبَّكَ بِمَا عَهِدَ عِندَكَ إِنَّنَا لَمُهۡتَدُونَ
43:49.en: And they said: O wizard! Entreat thy Lord for us by the pact that He hath made with thee. Lo! we verily will walk aright

43:50.ar: فَلَمَّا كَشَفۡنَا عَنۡهُمُ ٱلۡعَذَابَ إِذَا هُمۡ يَنكُثُونَ
43:50.en: But when We eased them of the torment, behold! they broke their word

43:51.ar: وَنَادَىٰ فِرۡعَوۡنُ فِي قَوۡمِهِۦ قَالَ يَٰقَوۡمِ أَلَيۡسَ لِي مُلۡكُ مِصۡرَ وَهَٰذِهِ ٱلۡأَنۡهَٰرُ تَجۡرِي مِن تَحۡتِيٓۚ أَفَلَا تُبۡصِرُونَ
43:51.en: And Pharaoh caused a proclamation to be made among his people saying: O my people! Is not mine the sovereignty of Egypt and these rivers flowing under me? Can ye not then discern

43:52.ar: أَمۡ أَنَا۠ خَيۡرࣱ مِّنۡ هَٰذَا ٱلَّذِي هُوَ مَهِينࣱ وَلَا يَكَادُ يُبِينُ
43:52.en: I am surely better than this fellow, who is despicable and can hardly make (his meaning) plain

43:53.ar: فَلَوۡلَآ أُلۡقِيَ عَلَيۡهِ أَسۡوِرَةࣱ مِّن ذَهَبٍ أَوۡ جَآءَ مَعَهُ ٱلۡمَلَٰٓئِكَةُ مُقۡتَرِنِينَ
43:53.en: Why, then, have armlets of gold not been set upon him, or angels sent along with him

43:54.ar: فَٱسۡتَخَفَّ قَوۡمَهُۥ فَأَطَاعُوهُۚ إِنَّهُمۡ كَانُواْ قَوۡمࣰ ا فَٰسِقِينَ
43:54.en: Thus he persuaded his people to make light (of Moses), and they obeyed him. Lo! they were a wanton folk

43:55.ar: فَلَمَّآ ءَاسَفُونَا ٱنتَقَمۡنَا مِنۡهُمۡ فَأَغۡرَقۡنَٰهُمۡ أَجۡمَعِينَ
43:55.en: So, when they angered Us, We punished them and drowned them every one

43:56.ar: فَجَعَلۡنَٰهُمۡ سَلَفࣰ ا وَمَثَلࣰ ا لِّلۡأٓخِرِينَ

6UNAaqwiDPc.title: Az-Zukhruf, Verses 46-56 (Fajr Dars)
6UNAaqwiDPc.one_line: Musa and Pharaoh in Az-Zukhruf: material miracles that convinced no one, Pharaoh's appeal to wealth and looks, and the same logic in politics, social media and marriage.
6UNAaqwiDPc.summary: Each surah tells a shared story its own way, and Az-Zukhruf tells Musa's to expose materialistic judgment. No dictator stands alone; Pharaoh's chiefs enabled him. Musa brought material signs, each greater than the last, plagues foretold to the day, yet they mocked him as a sorcerer, begged for relief and broke their promise nine times. Material miracles never convinced anyone, which is why this ummah was given the Quran, whose miracle is the change it makes in you. Pharaoh's answer was pure materialism: do I not own Egypt and its rivers, and am I not better than this lowly man who can barely speak? He attacked traits Musa did not control, not his message. We do the same today: people are objectified and judged by looks, politicians attack backgrounds instead of plans, and influencers outrank scientists. Pharaoh treated his people as fools and they obeyed because they had long accepted this value system. He asks whether we are part of that system, pointing to the rising age of marriage among Muslims in the West as young people chase standards no human can meet. Allah drowned the man who boasted of rivers beneath him. Even masajid fall into it when imams are chosen only for their voices.

outline.heading: Opening
Each surah tells a story its own way
outline.gist: Stories recur in the Quran but never identically; the differences follow each surah's theme, a key for anyone reflecting on the Quran.

outline.heading: Musa, the most mentioned prophet
outline.gist: His name appears over seventy times, far ahead of anyone else, because his story so resembles the Prophet's. He recites the passage on Pharaoh and his chiefs.

outline.heading: No dictator stands alone
outline.gist: There are always enablers. Musa declared himself a messenger of the Lord of the worlds and showed the staff and the shining hand, material signs they laughed at.

outline.heading: Each sign greater than the last
outline.gist: Every sign was clearer than the one before, and the signs turned into punishments in the hope they would return.

outline.heading: Plagues foretold in advance
outline.gist: Musa foretold each event, flood, drought, lice, frogs, blood, and it came exactly as he said; so why do people still ask for a material miracle?

outline.heading: Material miracles never convinced
outline.gist: Allah stopped sending such signs because every earlier people denied them; Salih's people saw a she-camel emerge from rock and slaughtered it. Materialism makes people less responsive to material miracles.

outline.heading: O sorcerer, pray to your Lord
outline.gist: They refused to see any layer beyond the material and recast him as a magician with his own god; Musa had been clear that he sought no wealth, control or status, only a change in how they saw things.

outline.heading: Broken promises, nine times
outline.gist: Locusts devoured only the Egyptians' crops as foretold; each time they begged for relief and went back on their word.

outline.heading: The miracle is you
outline.gist: This ummah was given the Quran instead, an ongoing miracle seen in the transformation of character it produces in whoever takes it to heart.

outline.heading: Do I not own Egypt and these rivers?
outline.gist: Growing desperate, Pharaoh pointed to his kingdom and the Nile's branches under his command, and to Musa's poverty; judged by one metric, he looked right.

outline.heading: This lowly one who can barely speak
outline.gist: Pharaoh mocked Musa's lack of status and his stutter, the reason Harun was his spokesman: traits he did not control that say nothing of his sincerity or honesty.

outline.heading: Objectification today
outline.gist: Images are more powerful than ever; people are judged on looks, appearance affects careers, and we have objectified and sexualized ourselves just as Pharaoh did.

outline.heading: Attack the person, not the plan
outline.gist: A child would reject Pharaoh's argument, yet political debates still answer a policy with someone's past, school or father, as when Obama was made to show his birth papers.

outline.heading: Influencers outrank scientists
outline.gist: Nothing has changed: social media rewards a look over talent, while scientists with real discoveries go unheard. May that not be how we see the world.

outline.heading: A speech found only here
outline.gist: This is the only place the Quran presents Pharaoh's words this way, and none of his points answer anything Musa said.

outline.heading: He made fools of his people, and they obeyed
outline.gist: Istakhaffa means he treated them with contempt using logic of no substance, and they followed; he points to the recent American presidency as a modern case.

outline.heading: A people already sold on materialism
outline.gist: They had long accepted that only money, power and status speak to them, so no one stood up to say it made no sense.

outline.heading: Are we part of this system?
outline.gist: We must withdraw from any system that enables materialistic valuing or pay a dire price; the rising marriage age among Western Muslims shows we are already paying.

outline.heading: Why marrying has become so hard
outline.gist: A decent person from a good family with some deen used to be enough; exposure to a materialistic society has made matches far harder.

outline.heading: Not only the money
outline.gist: He first blamed parents' financial demands but found singles who would pay anything still unmatched; arranged marriages, often mocked, reportedly last longer.

outline.heading: Standards no human can meet
outline.gist: We are all much the same; social media sets an inhuman standard that young people cannot meet without lies and surgery.

outline.heading: You are not immune
outline.gist: Whether seeking marriage or raising children, this will reach you unless the next generation's perspective changes. When they finally angered Allah, He took retribution.

outline.heading: The rivers above his head
outline.gist: He boasted of rivers beneath him, so the sea ran over him; they were drowned and made a precedent and example for later peoples.

outline.heading: A painful end for one-dimensional value
outline.gist: Basing value on wealth, status and power ends painfully; they knew his words were stupid but could not break the cycle, and we are being drawn into it.

outline.heading: Even in the masjid: judging imams by voice
outline.gist: Choosing imams for a beautiful voice alone is the same materialism; his most moving prayers were behind people with closeness to Allah, not great voices.

3:185.ar: كُلُّ نَفۡسࣲ ذَآئِقَةُ ٱلۡمَوۡتِۗ وَإِنَّمَا تُوَفَّوۡنَ أُجُورَكُمۡ يَوۡمَ ٱلۡقِيَٰمَةِۖ فَمَن زُحۡزِحَ عَنِ ٱلنَّارِ وَأُدۡخِلَ ٱلۡجَنَّةَ فَقَدۡ فَازَۗ وَمَا ٱلۡحَيَوٰةُ ٱلدُّنۡيَآ إِلَّا مَتَٰعُ ٱلۡغُرُورِ

4:78.en: Wheresoever ye may be, death will overtake you, even though ye were in lofty towers. Yet if a happy thing befalleth them they say: This is from Allah; and if an evil thing befalleth them they say: This is of thy doing (O Muhammad). Say (unto them): All is from Allah. 82J8VUa8F_4.speaker: adnan
82J8VUa8F_4.speaker_note: Fifth dars in his own Stages of the Hereafter series after Fajr at the Muslim Wellness Network
82J8VUa8F_4.title: Stages of the Hereafter 3: Death
82J8VUa8F_4.one_line: Death is certain, ordinary and even comforting; the Quran's verses on death and sleep help believers stop being surprised by it.
82J8VUa8F_4.summary: He presents death as the reminder that cuts through pleasure and the only advice a person really needs: the obituary notices that arrive by email will one day carry your own name. Echoing an early saying, a person is only a number of days, and each passing day removes part of him. Sleep is a nightly death in which Allah takes souls and returns those whose time has not come, so we already die every day, and there is nothing special about anyone's death. The verses on every soul tasting death define the real victory as being kept from the Fire and admitted to Paradise, with worldly life as a glittering distraction. When Allah told the Prophet, during ten hard years with Quraysh, that he would die and so would they, it was meant as comfort: oppressors do not escape accountability. Death finds people even in fortified towers because it needs no cause. He tells a story of Idris and the angel of death, noting such stories may be told but not used as evidence. Finally, fiction that imagines immortality always ends with people choosing to die; humans cannot even conceive of endlessness, so they should not be surprised that life ends.

outline.heading: Remembering the destroyer of pleasures
outline.gist: Keeping death in mind makes it hard to lose oneself in small worldly pleasures.

outline.heading: Death is enough of a reminder
outline.gist: Asked for advice, a righteous man would say to remember that you will pass away; the obituary notices that reach us will one day be about us.

outline.heading: You are only a number of days
outline.gist: An early saying describes the human as a handful of days, each one gone taking a part of you, and warns that worldly hopes turn out to be illusion.

outline.heading: Sleep as the lesser death
outline.gist: Allah takes souls at night and returns those whose term has not come; we die every day, and without that nightly death the body would fail.

outline.heading: There is nothing special about my death
outline.gist: Every human before us died and everyone alive will die; no one's death or lifespan is exceptional.

outline.heading: Every soul will taste death: the real victory
outline.gist: Whoever is kept from the Fire and admitted to Paradise has truly won; worldly life is glitter that distracts, a test of evil and good before the return to Allah.

outline.heading: You will die and they will die: comfort for the Prophet
outline.gist: After ten years of struggle with Quraysh, Allah reminded the Prophet that both he and his opponents would die, a comfort that no oppressor escapes accountability.

outline.heading: Death finds you even in lofty towers
outline.gist: Death needs no cause or trauma; isolation, protection or fortified castles cannot keep it out when its time comes.

outline.heading: Idris and the angel of death
outline.gist: Stories from the Children of Israel may be told but not used as evidence. Idris, urged by an angel friend to seek more time, was carried up to the heavens where the angel of death had been ordered to take his soul; nobody outruns Allah's decree.

outline.heading: Immortality cannot even be imagined
outline.gist: Every attempt in fiction to picture humans living forever ends with them choosing to die; we cannot conceive of endlessness, so why be surprised that life ends?

outline.heading: Outro

iUfiis4Y56U.speaker: adnan
iUfiis4Y56U.speaker_note: Second dars of his own Stages of the Hereafter series; refers back to yesterday's lesson and to his patients
iUfiis4Y56U.title: Stages of the Hereafter 2: Good and Bad Endings
iUfiis4Y56U.one_line: A person's ending reveals what they truly lived by, so purify the heart, keep secret deeds, and live ready to welcome death.
iUfiis4Y56U.summary: He calls a good ending the most important matter a Muslim can think about, and says it depends on letting go of the dunya, living in it as a stranger or traveller. He explains the hadith of the person who does the deeds of the people of Paradise until only an arm's length remains, when the decree overtakes him. He reads that decree as Allah's laws catching a hidden flaw: deeds done without sincerity while diseases of the heart were left untreated. The reverse also holds for someone trapped in a bad environment yet good inside. His scholars' image is a glass of milk with residue settled at the bottom, looking pure until the turbulence of the final moments stirs it up. Those who keep Allah's limits only when people are watching are at risk. Yaqub told his sons not to die except as Muslims because people choose their endings by how they live. He urges keeping a secret act of worship or charity, which the ego resists because it wants status. He closes with beautiful endings: Khadijah receiving salaam from her Lord, Bilal rejoicing at meeting his beloved companions, Abu Bakr correcting Aisha with a verse, and a patient who could only want more years.

outline.heading: Opening
A good ending depends on letting go of the dunya
outline.gist: Securing a good ending makes everything else trivial, and the key is not clinging to a worldly life we invest so heavily in.

outline.heading: A stranger or a traveller in this world
outline.gist: The Prophet's instruction to live in the world as a foreigner or someone passing through for a set time.

outline.heading: Deeds of Paradise until the decree overtakes
outline.gist: The authentic hadith of one who does the deeds of the people of Paradise until something flips him at the end, and its reverse.

outline.heading: The hidden flaw that flips the scales
outline.gist: He reads the decree as Allah's laws of judgement catching something hidden, such as deeds done all life without sincerity while diseases of the heart grew untreated.

outline.heading: The reverse: goodness trapped in a bad environment
outline.gist: Someone raised in a terrible environment but good inside, struggling to escape the spiral, may be allowed to turn at the end, because what is truly inside surfaces at the close.

outline.heading: The glass of milk and its residue
outline.gist: His teachers' image: residue settles and the milk looks pure until turbulence mixes it; the final moments are that turbulence, so rid yourself of the residue beforehand.

outline.heading: Those who break Allah's limits when alone
outline.gist: The Prophet described people who pray at night like everyone else but violate Allah's limits when only He sees them; this hidden habit can flip their last minutes.

outline.heading: Yaqub's counsel: you choose your ending
outline.gist: Yaqub told his sons not to die except as Muslims because the ending is the sum of how one lived; Allah does not break a sincere life's pattern at the last moment.

outline.heading: Keep a secret with Allah
outline.gist: Have an act of worship nobody knows about, like the man in the shade of Allah who gave charity so secretly his left hand did not know what his right gave.

outline.heading: Secret charity and the ego's resistance
outline.gist: Giving so that not even the recipient knows will be the hardest fight of your life, because the ego is programmed to seek status and cannot understand a deed with no visible reward.

outline.heading: Khadijah's farewell: salaam from her Lord
outline.gist: Jibreel came without revelation to convey Allah's salaam to Khadijah and glad tidings of a hollow-jewel palace in Paradise without noise or fatigue, after a life spent in a loud, demanding household.

outline.heading: Bilal: tomorrow I meet the beloved ones
outline.gist: As his wife lamented, Bilal told her to call it a joyful day because he would soon meet Muhammad and his companions.

outline.heading: Abu Bakr corrects Aisha at his deathbed
outline.gist: When Aisha recited a line about wealth availing nothing at death, Abu Bakr told her to recite instead the verse about the stupor of death arriving with the truth.

outline.heading: Life as preparation to welcome death
outline.gist: The righteous all had meaningful final moments because they lived accepting death; everything in life should prepare us not just to be ready for it but to welcome it.

outline.heading: The patient who wanted a few more years
outline.gist: A very ill patient in his nineties, asked what he hoped for, could only say a few more years, then a few more; people refuse to accept the one certain fact, though acceptance, not longing for death, is what is asked.

outline.heading: The great names all welcomed the moment
outline.gist: From the prophets to the companions, their deaths show the same pattern of calm acceptance because they had prepared all their lives.

outline.heading: Outro

Bvlt1VEwKMo.speaker: adnan
Bvlt1VEwKMo.speaker_note: Post-Fajr dars at Muslim Wellness Network on his own channel, continuing his explanation of the surah
Bvlt1VEwKMo.title: Az-Zukhruf, Verses 66-80 (Fajr Dars)
Bvlt1VEwKMo.one_line: The Hour erases material value: friendships for gain turn to enmity, Jannah's real treasure is freedom from fear and grief, and the truth was hated for its cost.
Bvlt1VEwKMo.summary: Recapping the surah's case against judging everything by financial value, from the treatment of women to Pharaoh's boast, he notes that such logic still wins elections today, and that Isa, who owned nothing, is now remembered with the most consumerist day of the year. Not all materialism is wrong, though; the closing verses show where it belongs. When the Hour comes nothing material remains, so a value system built on wealth dies instantly, as anyone who has lost a fortune and watched people stop noticing them can attest. Friends become enemies that day except the pious, because friendships built on gain fall apart, while those who loved one another for Allah sit on pulpits of light. He asks people to audit their friendships and to be greedy for the hereafter rather than the world. The greatest reward is spiritual: no fear and no grief, the only things that ruin a day, which is why happiness must come from the inside. Jannah is not boring: it is life with discovery, building and even competition, minus fear and grief, and its pleasures are real. The people of the Fire beg Malik to end them because they hated the truth, which always costs something. Every whisper is recorded.

outline.heading: Opening
A finale for the twenty-first century
outline.gist: As materialism becomes the only accepted metric, the surah insists this is not how Allah made the universe, how you should judge yourself or others; it began with how Jahiliyyah devalued women.

outline.heading: Recap: from ancestral custom to Pharaoh's boast
outline.gist: Blind following of lucrative custom, Ibrahim's opposition, the demand for a great man of the two towns, the silver houses withheld, and Pharaoh claiming Egypt and its rivers against a man without wealth.

outline.heading: Pharaoh's logic still works
outline.gist: His argument was irrelevant to the point Musa made, yet people responded, and he notes they still do, citing a recent American president.

outline.heading: Isa owned nothing, and now a consumer holiday
outline.gist: The Quran's example of asceticism walked through the world possessing nothing, yet he was turned into an object of worship and his birthday into the biggest spending day on earth. Not all materialism is wrong, as the coming verses show.

outline.heading: What are they waiting for but the Hour?
outline.gist: That moment wrecks every law we know; we come out of graves without clothing, homes or phones, so a value system based on wealth is flushed away instantly.

outline.heading: How quickly the ruined rich are forgotten
outline.gist: Someone who loses inherited wealth goes from open doors to being unnoticed; Muslims must refuse to judge or be judged that way.

outline.heading: Friends that day will be enemies

yHAfvcxfdy4.title: Az-Zukhruf, Verses 81-89 (Fajr Dars)
yHAfvcxfdy4.one_line: Closing Ramadan by offering something to others, then the surah's final dare to prove Allah has a son, the evidence for God, and forgiving those who refuse.
yHAfvcxfdy4.summary: In the last dars of Ramadan he first reflects on the month: a younger crowd came by choice, a sign that the older generation has underestimated what is possible and must now mentor and support them, and sisters must carry half the work, as Khadijah did. Ramadan should be a beginning: you hold onto your deen by offering something to others now rather than waiting until you feel good enough, because helping others is what reforms you. He urges a heartfelt dua in the last hour before Maghrib. Completing the surah, he calls verse 81 unique in the Quran: if the Most Merciful had a son, the Prophet would be the first to worship him, a dare to bring evidence. Muslims follow evidence wherever it points, but seeking God in a laboratory is looking in the wrong place, since a God that science could prove would not be God. The evidence lies in one system running from atom to galaxy, life's unexplained will to live, prophets in every civilization and moments in one's own life. He warns against living on the hope of intercession, marvels at DNA as Allah's code, and reads the Prophet's anguished complaint that his people will not believe. The answer is to forgive them, never envy their worldly wealth, and give them salam, a real commitment of peace.

outline.gist: Young people are not dragged to this as they are to other things; it shows the community has underestimated what it can do, and the older generation must chaperone, mentor and support them.

outline.heading: Hold onto your deen by offering

outline.heading: Helping others makes you better

outline.heading: A dua in the last hour before Maghrib
outline.gist: On the last day, set aside the final hour to pour out to Allah who you want to be after Ramadan; he does it every year.

outline.heading: If the Most Merciful had a son
outline.gist: A verse without parallel in the Quran: if you can prove Allah has a son, the Prophet would be the first to worship.

outline.heading: Show me your evidence
outline.gist: Those who would rather God be less powerful and less demanding of accountability are dared to bring proof for lowering His status.

outline.heading: Every civilization had a temple
outline.gist: Some civilizations lacked schools but all had temples and a prophet with the same message; people rejected it because it was not lucrative, and Islam costs the one who commits to it.

outline.heading: A Muslim follows evidence wherever it points
outline.gist: It is strange for a Muslim to see clear evidence, even about health, and not follow it; our minds are meant to embrace proof.

outline.heading: Looking for God in the wrong place
outline.gist: Islam never asks for blind following; asking science for God is a category error, since science measures only the observable universe in time and space.

outline.heading: A God science could prove would not be God
outline.gist: Whatever is contained in time and space is not God, because then time and space would encompass Him.

outline.heading: One system from atom to galaxy
outline.gist: The verses are exaltation; the evidence is that everything orbits a centre in the same way, from the atom to the galaxy to the tawaf, pointing to one source.

outline.heading: Why does life want to live?
outline.gist: Science studies how the first cell worked but not why life wants to live and always finds a way; a newborn wants to breathe without being taught.

outline.heading: Tawhid is too pure for the ego
outline.gist: Every people from South America to Japan received prophets; tawhid is selfless, equalises everyone, frees you from others and is not lucrative for the wealthy, so people resist it.

outline.heading: Your own life as evidence
outline.gist: Moments when everything should have gone wrong and something turned it are evidence enough; denial is comfortable because it removes accountability, so leave them to their play.

outline.heading: God in the heavens and God on earth
outline.gist: Against the idea of one god above and many on earth: He is God in both, blessed, sovereign, with knowledge of the Hour; intercession only with His permission and for the truth.

outline.heading: Do not live on hope of intercession
outline.gist: Hoping for the Prophet's intercession is right, but a good name will not carry you; he may lift a nine to ten, not a two to ten.

outline.heading: A surah that ends in exaltation
outline.gist: A surah about materialistic values ends with a brave dare; even scientists without religion admit some force behind existence.

outline.heading: He coded your DNA
outline.gist: That force is Allah, who cared enough to communicate; we only recently learned to code, while He has been coding life in DNA since creation.

outline.heading: All life is related
outline.gist: We share DNA with trees, grass and monkeys, so there is nothing to be offended by; He is sending messages every day.

outline.heading: Every experience carries a message
outline.gist: We are poor at decoding; he reads the thirst he saw this month as a sign that he is not doing enough. Asked who created them, they say Allah.

outline.heading: O my Lord, these people will not believe
outline.gist: The sentence leaves part unsaid; ya rabb is the cry of complaint and pain when no one stands with you, which is why we use it in salah.

outline.heading: When your own family will not listen
outline.gist: The Prophet's heart ached as his uncle and people refused; you may feel the same about a son, daughter or brother who will not come.

outline.heading: Turn aside and forgive
outline.gist: Do not bully, hate, cut off or burn bridges; tell the believers to forgive those who have no interest in Allah, and never envy anyone's worldly possessions.

outline.heading: Envy only those ahead in Quran and dawah
outline.gist: Those drowning in a materialistic life are not happy; you need only enough not to be in need, so pity and forgive them instead.

outline.heading: Asleep in sujood in Syria
outline.gist: He recalls a painfully slow night prayer in Syria during which a friend fell asleep in sujood; the fatigue of these nights is precious because it is for Allah alone.

outline.heading: Salam: a commitment of peace
outline.gist: In the desert strangers fought to the death out of fear; salam declares that nothing but peace will come from you, a commitment returned by the other.

outline.heading: They will come to know
outline.gist: If you could not guide them, forgive them and give them peace; one day their materialistic value system will prove useless and they will know.

drwfPeZU75o.title: Stages of the Hereafter 6: The Death of the Believer
drwfPeZU75o.one_line: Walking through the long hadith of the soul's journey: how a believer dies, ascends, is questioned, and rests in the barzakh.
drwfPeZU75o.summary: He begins walking through the stages after death using the long hadith in the collections of Ahmad and Abu Dawud, one of the few very long narrations he considers authentic. The Prophet sat at an Ansari's unfinished grave, scratched the ground with a stick and told the companions three times to seek refuge from the punishment of the grave. Every transition is painful, like birth, but for the believer angels with sun-bright faces descend with a shroud and perfume from Paradise, and the angel of death calls the good soul to Allah's forgiveness and pleasure. It flows out like a drop from a jug's spout, all in an instant, since time there is relative. The soul rises with the scent of musk, greeted at each heaven by the names it loved most, until Allah orders its record placed among the highest and returns it to the earth. He explains barzakh as a reality that relates to this world as this world relates to the womb. In the grave the believer answers the questions about his Lord, religion and Prophet, the grave is widened and furnished from Paradise, his deeds appear in beautiful form, and he is shown the place in Hell he was spared. He urges seeking refuge in Allah and preparing for this journey.

outline.heading: Opening
Familiarity with what is coming
outline.gist: The series aims to make listeners familiar and comfortable with death's process, narrated through the hadith in the collections of Ahmad and Abu Dawud.

outline.heading: At the grave of a man of the Ansar
outline.gist: The companions accompanied the Prophet to a funeral where the grave was not yet ready, as people walk to nearby cemeteries in many Muslim lands.

outline.heading: Seek refuge from the punishment of the grave
outline.gist: The Prophet scratched the ground with a stick and told them three times to seek refuge from the grave's punishment; this is one of the few very long hadith that are authentic.

outline.heading: Every transition is painful
outline.gist: Birth from the womb into the world hurts though it is beautiful, and leaving the world is the same.

outline.heading: Angels with faces like the sun
outline.gist: Angels descend carrying a shroud and perfume from Paradise and sit where the dying believer can see them.

outline.heading: Time is relative at death
outline.gist: All of this may happen in a split second, even in a sudden death; onlookers see nothing and do not realize how close Allah and His angels are.

outline.heading: The call to the good soul
outline.gist: The angel of death sits at the head and, at the last breath, calls the good soul out to its Lord's forgiveness and pleasure.

outline.heading: Like a drop from a spout
outline.gist: The soul leaves as easily as a single drop leaving a jug's spout, and the waiting angels take it from the angel of death in a blink.

outline.heading: The soul is never neglected
outline.gist: The verse he recites shows the angels entrusted with souls do not neglect their task; the soul is returned to its Lord.

outline.heading: The spirit and the scent of musk
outline.gist: Little is known about the spirit, so he avoids speculating; the believer's soul leaves with the finest scent of musk, while the earthly body smells of earth.

outline.heading: Called by the names you loved most
outline.gist: As the soul ascends, it is addressed by the name or title that always pleased it in life.

outline.heading: Passing through the heavens
outline.gist: Permission is granted at each heaven, and the angels nearest to Allah join the procession up to the seventh heaven.

outline.heading: Recorded among the highest, returned to the earth
outline.gist: Allah orders the servant's record placed among the highest ranks and the soul returned to the earth from which humans were created and will be raised.

outline.heading: Barzakh is to this world as this world is to the womb
outline.gist: The realm after death cannot be described in words, just as an infant who knows only the womb could not grasp the world.

outline.heading: Interlude
The questioning in the grave
outline.gist: The returned soul is asked about its Lord, religion and the man sent to it, and answers that it believed in Allah, followed the Prophet and lived by the Book.

outline.heading: A truthful servant's grave furnished from Paradise
outline.gist: A call from heaven confirms the servant spoke the truth; he is clothed and furnished from Paradise and his grave is widened as far as the eye can see.

outline.heading: Good deeds in beautiful form
outline.gist: A beautiful, fragrant figure brings glad tidings and reveals itself as the person's good deeds.

outline.heading: Shown the Fire he was spared, then Paradise
outline.gist: He is shown his place in Hell had he displeased Allah, then that door closes and the door to Paradise opens with its breeze and his waiting family.

outline.heading: Forgetting the barzakh at resurrection
outline.gist: When people are resurrected they forget much, and the best estimate among them is that they stayed only a day.

outline.heading: Barzakh means what lies between
outline.gist: In Arabic barzakh is anything between two things: a transitional existence before what comes next.

outline.heading: The grave as a realm, not a hole
outline.gist: Even the unburied enter it, since it is a realm rather than a place; he avoids the scholarly disputes and sticks to the texts.

outline.heading: Allah dislikes troubling the believer
outline.gist: The Prophet saw nothing worse than the grave, yet for the believer it is a celebration; Allah dislikes grieving the believer at death, but it is His decree.

outline.heading: Outro

WOrOFs-8ueE.title: Stages of the Hereafter 4: Death, Part 2
WOrOFs-8ueE.one_line: Why believers fear death, what continues after it, and how the Quran describes its fixed time, stupor and finality.
WOrOFs-8ueE.summary: He asks why people fear death. For most it is the dread of nothingness, but a Muslim's fear should be different: either part of us doubts there is anything next, or, more properly, death ends every chance to repent and fix mistakes. Only three things keep adding to the scales afterwards: charity that outlives you, beneficial knowledge, and children who pray for you. He then tells of Caliph Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik asking a scholar in Medina why people hate death. The answer: they built their worldly life and neglected the next, so they dread moving from the built to the ruined. The righteous meet Allah like a traveller coming home, the disobedient like a runaway slave returned, and each should measure himself against the Quran. The conversation is said to have shaped Sulayman's choice of Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz as successor. Verses follow on death's fixed time, the angels being nearer the dying than the family at the bedside, the plea to be sent back being refused, the stupor of death, and death waiting ahead of the one fleeing it. He ends by noting that no one remembers their grandfather's grandfather, so preparing calmly for that moment is each person's own concern.

outline.heading: The fear of nothingness
outline.gist: Most people fear death as the idea of no longer existing while the world carries on without them; Muslims do not believe this, so why do they still fear it?

outline.heading: Why Muslims fear death: a hidden doubt
outline.gist: The first reason is that part of us may not fully believe there is something after.

outline.heading: Why Muslims fear death: no more chance to repent
outline.gist: The proper reason is that death ends every chance to rectify mistakes; now Allah comes running to whoever walks to Him, but after death you remain conscious and nothing you do counts.

outline.heading: Deeds that continue: charity that outlives you
outline.gist: The Prophet said deeds stop at death except three; the first is charity or a project whose benefit keeps flowing to people.

outline.heading: Deeds that continue: beneficial knowledge
outline.gist: Any useful knowledge people keep benefiting from after you are gone.

outline.heading: Deeds that continue: a child who prays for you
outline.gist: Raising a generation that remembers you and makes dua for you.

outline.heading: Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik's legacy
outline.gist: On his Hajj the caliph sought out a scholar in Medina; his lasting service to the ummah was naming Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz as successor instead of his own son, reportedly partly because of this conversation.

outline.heading: Why we hate death: a built dunya and a neglected hereafter
outline.gist: No one wants to leave a beautiful, well-built home for one with nothing in it.

outline.heading: Meeting Allah: homecoming or a runaway returned
outline.gist: The righteous meet Allah like a long-absent traveller reuniting with family; the disobedient like a runaway slave brought back to his master.

outline.heading: Measure your deeds against the Book of Allah
outline.gist: Asked what awaits him with Allah, the scholar told the caliph to weigh his deeds against what the Quran says of the righteous and the wicked.

outline.heading: Death arrives exactly on time
outline.gist: When a person's term comes it is neither delayed nor brought forward by a moment; it was decreed before their first breath.

outline.heading: Closer than those at the bedside
outline.gist: Allah and His angels are nearer to the dying than relatives standing by the bed; whoever denies God is challenged to bring the soul back.

outline.heading: Send me back: the plea refused
outline.gist: The dying person begs to return for one moment to repent and get it right, and hears a firm no; once the soul leaves it never returns.

outline.heading: The unknown hour and the stupor of death
outline.gist: No one knows what they will earn tomorrow or where they will die; death's stupor is an overwhelming intoxication that comes with the truth people ran from.

outline.heading: The death you flee is waiting ahead
outline.gist: Death is not behind you; it waits at the end of the line you are running along.

outline.heading: An admonition from a classical book on death
outline.gist: A scholar's address to the deluded: think of death's bitter cup and the just Judge; loved ones will leave, friends betray, and the hoarder takes only his shroud and his sins to one who will not excuse him.

outline.heading: Who remembers your grandfather's grandfather?
outline.gist: Someone asked could barely name his great-great-grandfather, though he exists because of him; we become irrelevant very quickly, even to our own descendants.

outline.heading: Be ready with no regrets
outline.gist: Since no one else will care about that moment, prepare all your life so you can pass on calmly and without regret.
